pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000 (a synthesising META-topic).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above' — i.e. the applied capstone over the Y6 place-value objectives (to 10,000,000, rounding, negatives).
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): draws on 4.NBT.A (read/write/compare/round multi-digit), 5.NBT.A (place value, rounding) and 6.NS.C (negatives in context) applied to problem contexts.
• Operational details: Pose realistic multi-step problems — populations, distances, temperatures, sea depths, attendances — that require choosing WHICH place-value skill to deploy (round for a headline, compare/order to rank, use negatives for depths). Emphasise sense-making: estimate first by rounding, then check the exact answer is reasonable, and interpret the result back in context (a rounded headline vs an exact count).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Population 8,274,500 — round to the nearest million for a headline.' Tier B: 'Order three ocean-trench depths given as negatives.' Tier C: 'Estimate total attendance at three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000 and judge if your estimate is over or under.'
bestPractices: Use authentic large-number contexts (populations, distances, depths, attendances) so pupils choose the appropriate place-value tool rather than being told which
Teach estimate-first: round to get a ballpark, then compute/compare exactly and check reasonableness against the estimate
Require interpretation back in context — when is a rounded headline appropriate, when is the exact figure needed
Blend the sub-skills within a single problem (round AND order AND read negatives) to build flexible selection
Model judging whether a rounded estimate is an over- or under-estimate, connecting rounding direction to context
keyRepresentations: Number line / magnitude bars for ordering and rounding seven-digit values
Period-grouped place-value chart for reading and writing the numbers in play
Vertical number line for negative contexts (depths, temperatures)
Estimation strips pairing rounded values with the exact figures
commonMisconceptions: Applying a rounding rule mechanically without checking the answer makes sense in context
Ordering by digit count or face value rather than aligned place value for seven-digit numbers
Mishandling negatives in context (ranking −900 m as shallower than −300 m)
Rounding to the wrong place for the purpose (nearest 10 when a million is asked for a headline)
Losing placeholder zeros when reading/writing the large numbers within a problem

learn.summary: Applied capstone for place value to 10,000,000: learners choose and combine place-value tools — rounding to a stated place, ordering/comparing seven-digit and negative numbers, and reading/writing with placeholder zeros — within realistic multi-step problems (populations, distances, temperatures, sea depths, attendances). Core habit: estimate first by rounding, compute/compare exactly, then interpret the result back in context and judge whether an estimate is over or under.

activities.title: Large-number problem workspace: pick the right tool
feedback: If a learner rounds 8,274,500 to 9,000,000 'because the rest is big', have them underline the millions digit and box only the single digit to its right (2); state 'only that one digit decides' and locate the number on a line between 8,000,000 and 9,000,000.

If a learner ranks -7,921 m as deepest because '7 thousand is the smallest number', use a vertical number line with 0 at sea level to show that -9,052 m, the most negative reading, sits furthest below zero, so it is deepest and least in value.

If rounded parts come out the wrong order of magnitude (e.g. reading 214,600 as 21,460), rebuild the period structure (ones, thousands, millions) on a place-value grid and read each number aloud by period before rounding.

To decide whether an estimate is over or under, check each addend: did it round up or down, and by how much? Add up the up-adjustments and the down-adjustments and compare them — the estimate is over when the ups outweigh the downs and under when the downs outweigh the ups. Note that rounding can go in mixed directions: for 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700 to the nearest 100,000, 214,600 rounds down while 388,050 and 96,700 round up, and here the ups slightly outweigh the down, giving a small over-estimate (700,000 vs exact 699,350).
activities.rationale: The objective is choosing and combining place-value skills in context, so an open workspace where learners select a tool, see the consequence and self-check against an estimate is proposed to target that selection skill directly. An optional interactive version can offer a magnitude number line, a rounding bracket that snaps to a chosen place, comparison/ordering slots, a negative-scale toggle, and an over/under flag on the estimate — these make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same work can be done on paper with a drawn number line and place-value grid.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000.
Applied place-value problem solving draws on read/write/compare/round of multi-digit numbers (4.NBT.A, 5.NBT.A) and negatives in context (6.NS.C).
learnerActions: Load a scenario with mixed demands, e.g. three ocean trenches at -8,376 m, -9,052 m and -7,921 m plus a country's population of 8,274,500 needed for a news headline.

For the headline, round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and state the result (8,000,000); name the single digit that decided the rounding (the hundred-thousands digit, 2) and explain why the digits after it do not change the decision.

Order the three trench depths from deepest to shallowest, placing each on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level, and justify ordering by position (more negative = lower = deeper), not by comparing the digits while ignoring the minus sign.

Estimate a combined attendance for three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000, then compute the exact total and state whether your rounded estimate came out over or under, explaining how you can tell.
Say back in context which figure each situation needs: a rounded headline for the population, exact negatives for ranking the trenches.
activities.intendedInsight: The same set of numbers can demand different place-value tools — rounding for a headline, exact negatives for a ranking — and estimating first tells you whether the exact answer is believable.

activities.title: Fluency check on the component skills
feedback: For ordering: the correct deepest-to-shallowest order for -4,000, -10,900, -7,200 is -10,900, -7,200, -4,000, because more negative is lower (further below sea level).
For the estimate: rounding to the nearest 100,000 gives 200,000 + 400,000 + 100,000 = about 700,000; then check the exact total (699,350) is close to it.
For rounding to the nearest million: the deciding digit is the hundred-thousands digit (2), so 8,274,500 rounds down to 8,000,000, not up to 9,000,000.
activities.rationale: The component skills are cleanly assessable, so short targeted items are a useful companion for checking applied fluency. These items check recognition and execution of each skill; on their own they do not elicit the open multi-step tool-selection that the workspace activity targets.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000.
learnerActions: Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and choose the correct result.
Order three negative trench depths (e.g. -4,000 m, -10,900 m, -7,200 m) from deepest to shallowest.
Estimate a total attendance (e.g. 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700) by rounding each to the nearest 100,000.
activities.intendedInsight: Each component place-value skill — rounding to a stated place, ordering negatives by position, estimating by rounding addends — can be executed accurately on its own.

activities.title: Framing contexts before computing
feedback: If a learner rounds a figure to the wrong place for the purpose (e.g. nearest 10 for a headline about millions), ask what level of precision a reader needs and point them to the relevant period.

If they would round depths used for a ranking, remind them that ranking needs the exact ordering, so the comparison should use exact values: rounding (even consistently to the same place) can make different depths equal, e.g. -8,376 m and -8,420 m both round to -8,000 m to the nearest thousand, so the order is lost.
activities.rationale: Framing and discussion build the sense-making and interpretation the topic emphasises; a dialogue can coach problem framing, while the compute-and-check work is best carried out in the workspace, so this activity should lead into, not replace, the workspace task.
learnerActions: Study a labelled population/depth chart or world map and tap or point to regions to reveal exact figures.
For each figure, state what you would round it to for a fair headline, and which figures you would keep exact for ranking.
Take on a journalist's brief: turn a set of exact figures into fair rounded headlines, then explain why the rounded version is appropriate for a headline but not for a precise ranking.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which place-value tool a situation calls for — and whether a rounded headline or an exact figure is appropriate — is itself part of the problem.

constraints: Use authentic large-number contexts (populations, distances, depths, attendances) so learners choose the appropriate place-value tool rather than being told which.

Teach estimate-first: round for a ballpark, then compute/compare exactly and check reasonableness against the estimate; require interpreting the result back in context (when a rounded headline suffices vs when the exact figure is needed).
Blend sub-skills within a single problem (round AND order AND read negatives) to build flexible selection.
Recognition/short-answer items check component fluency but do not on their own elicit the open multi-step tool selection; use them as a companion, not a substitute.

A static chart cannot host the compute-and-check work, and a dialogue is better suited to coaching problem framing than to carrying the full multi-step working; treat these as scaffolds leading into the problem-solving rather than substitutes.

Any interactive features (snapping rounding bracket, draggable number line, negative-scale toggle, over/under flag) are optional ways to make the mechanism visible; the same learning can occur on paper with a drawn number line and place-value grid.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked numbers: 8,274,500 rounds to 8,000,000 (deciding hundred-thousands digit 2 -> round down) — correct. Ordering -4,000, -10,900, -7,200 deepest-to-shallowest = -10,900, -7,200, -4,000 — correct. Estimate 214,600+388,050+96,700 rounded to nearest 100,000 = 200,000+400,000+100,000 = 700,000; exact = 699,350, so the estimate is a slight over-estimate (by 650) — consistent; up-adjustments (11,950 + 3,300 = 15,250) exceed the down-adjustment (14,600) by 650.

The over/under feedback in Activity 1 handles the mixed-rounding case correctly: learners weigh total up-adjustments against total down-adjustments rather than assuming all addends round the same way.

The second CCSS source is marked verified:false in the row; the standards mapping (4.NBT.A/5.NBT.A/6.NS.C) is retained as sourced but its verification status is unconfirmed, and no claim of medium effectiveness rests on it.
The probe 'Why is -10,900 m deeper than -4,000 m when 10,900 is the bigger number?' is pedagogically sound and is reflected via the number-line position argument in the ordering feedback.

probeDeeper: For the rounding, which single digit made the decision, and why did the rest not matter?
Why is -10,900 m deeper than -4,000 m when 10,900 is the bigger number?
Would your estimate be too high or too low compared with the exact total — how can you tell?
What if the reading had been 8,724,500 — would it still round to 8,000,000?

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds using the wrong place — looks at a later digit or rounds 8,274,500 up to 9,000,000 because 'the rest is big', instead of reading the hundred-thousands digit (2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Underline the millions digit and box the single digit to its right; state the rule 'only that one digit decides'. Model on a number line between 8,000,000 and 9,000,000.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds to 9,000,000, or hesitates over which digit decides; cannot name the deciding digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders the negative depths by magnitude, treating -4,000 as deepest because '4 thousand is the smallest number'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level; show -10,900 sits furthest below zero, so it is deepest and least in value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks -4,000 as deepest / -10,900 as shallowest, ignoring that more-negative is lower.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the periods in the seven-digit numbers — misplaces commas or reads 214,600 as 21,460 / 2,146,000, so the estimate is off by a factor of ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the period structure (ones, thousands, millions) with a place-value grid; read each number aloud by period before rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounded parts are the wrong order of magnitude; total estimate is 70,000 or 7,000,000.

responseLevels.gap: Rounds on the wrong digit, orders negatives by magnitude, or produces an estimate of the wrong order of magnitude.
responseLevels.full: Executes all three fluently — names the deciding digit when rounding, orders negatives by number-line position, rounds each addend before summing, and can say whether the estimate is over or under.
responseLevels.partial: Completes one or two tasks correctly (often the rounding) but cannot reliably order the negatives or justify the estimate's direction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Three tasks laid out on paper. (1) Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million. (2) Three ocean-trench readings are -4,000 m, -10,900 m and -7,200 m; order them from deepest to shallowest. (3) Estimate 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700 by rounding each first.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch the working, not the answers. Correct rounding requires looking at the digit to the RIGHT of the millions place (2 → round down) — a child who rounds on the wrong digit or rounds up 'because there's lots after it' is exposed. The negatives task separates children who order by magnitude (calling -4,000 deepest) from those who order by position on the number line. The estimate reveals whether they round before adding or add then round.
